extracted.intended_audience: inventors, applicants and patent practitioners seeking to file an international (PCT) patent application
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing, filing and prosecuting an international patent application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT): who may file, what a PCT application must contain, required fees, filing languages/methods, procedural steps (formalities check, international search, publication, optional preliminary examination) and national-phase entry requirements and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to file a PCT application
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file an international application under the PCT (also called “PCT application”) if you are a national or resident of a country that is a PCT Contracting State. If your PCT application includes more than one applicant, only one of those applicants must meet this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent receiving Office for filing
rubrics_metrics.description: You should file with a patent Office that is competent to receive your PCT application (known as a PCT “receiving Office”). This is usually the patent Office in the country of your nationality or residence. Applicants from any Contracting State can also choose to file with the International Bureau of WIPO. Applicants in some countries may need to get national security clearance before filing with the International Bureau.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees payable on filing (types and payment rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must pay three fees to the receiving Office when filing your PCT application: an international filing fee, a search fee (varies by ISA) and a transmittal fee (varies by receiving Office). All the above fees should be paid in full to the receiving Office, in the currency and via the payment method accepted by that Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current international filing fee cited as 1,330 Swiss francs (may be increased if your application has more than 30 pages, and may be reduced if you file electronically). Applicants from certain States are entitled to fee reductions. For exact amounts refer to the PCT Fee Tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of a PCT application
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, a PCT application requires most of the same data as a national patent application. A PCT application must include: a request (including bibliographic data about the applicant(s)); a description (written disclosure of the invention); one or more claims (defining the scope of protection sought from the application); one or more drawings (where required); and an abstract (summary of the invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language requirements for filing
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file a PCT application in any language accepted by the receiving Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PCT application is in a language not used by the ISA, you will be required to submit a translation in a language accepted by that ISA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted means of filing and recommendation to use ePCT
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptable means of filing depends on your receiving Office. Most Offices accept the filing of international applications electronically or on paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO has developed an online system, ePCT, to help applicants prepare, file and manage their PCT applications, and it is accepted by a wide range of receiving Offices. WIPO recommends that you use ePCT to prepare and file your PCT application wherever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities check by the receiving Office
rubrics_metrics.description: The receiving Office will first check whether your application can be accorded an international filing date, namely, whether the applicant is entitled to file a PCT application and whether the application contains all the essential elements (PCT Article 11(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It will further determine whether all the other PCT formality requirements are complied with (PCT Article 14 and Rule 11) and all the required fees have been paid, and if not yet, invite you to make corrections and/or pay missing fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: International search and written opinion by the ISA
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Searching Authority (ISA) selected in your PCT application will produce a search report (identifying published patent documents and technical literature that may influence whether your invention is patentable) and a written opinion containing detailed analysis of your invention’s potential patentability based on a set of criteria set forth for the PCT purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You receive a copy of these two documents about 4 months after filing your PCT application. The findings and opinions in these reports provide both you and the national Offices with helpful information on your invention’s potential patentability but are not legally binding for the national Offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: International publication timing and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as possible after the expiration of 18 months from the priority date, WIPO publishes your international application together with the search report on PATENTSCOPE, WIPO’s patent database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After publication, you will have additional time to consider the information in the search report and decide if you want to continue pursuing patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Preliminary Examination (optional) — scope and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In this optional procedure, an International Preliminary Examining Authority (IPEA) carries out an additional patentability analysis on your application. You may file amendments to your application during this procedure (in light of the search report and written opinion of the ISA you have received), and ask the IPEA to conduct the examination on the application as amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final outcome of this procedure is an examination report providing opinions on the potential patentability of your invention based on PCT standards. Additional costs apply for this examination. This report, like the written opinion of the ISA, is also non-binding, but may provide you with additional or updated patentability analysis to further help you decide whether you would like to continue pursuing your application in the national phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: National phase entry requirements and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of the PCT procedure patents can only be granted by each of the national Offices in the national phase. If you do not pursue your application in the national phase within the required time limit (usually 30 months from the priority date), your PCT application will lapse and lose its effect in the national Offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you decide to further seek a patent grant in certain countries, you will need to perform, within the applicable time limit, the required actions before each national (or regional) Office: usually providing a translation of your PCT application in the language accepted by the particular national Office, paying the required fees, and appointing a local patent representative. The national Office will then examine the substance of your patent application to decide whether a patent can be granted according to its own law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key PCT timing milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical PCT procedural timeframes referenced: international search documents are received about 4 months after filing; international publication occurs as soon as possible after 18 months from the priority date; national phase entry is usually required within 30 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines may vary by Office and circumstance; consult specific national/regional Offices and PCT Fee Tables for exact timing and any extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of using the PCT system
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the PCT to seek patent protection for your invention internationally can be advantageous: it is more convenient than filing separate national patent applications; gives you more time to decide whether to pursue national filings; provides expert opinions on potential patentability; and can save effort and unnecessary cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are practical benefits to consider when deciding whether to use the PCT route; they do not change national Offices' substantive grant criteria.
